title: One minute of short questions
summary: Learn the two chairs of cross-examination, take a minute of a parent's hardest questions about the price you chose with your table in your hand, then argue whether charging more than a thing cost you is wrong at all.
materials: your printed profit table from Build, and your chosen price with its date on it
a parent with twenty minutes and no mercy

steps.title: The two chairs
steps.body:
Cross-examination is the only part of a debate where the other side gets to talk back mid-sentence, and it is the part most people are worst at, in both chairs. One minute each way, a shared clock, and no speeches allowed from either of you.

In the asking chair. Keep every question shorter than one breath. A long question is a speech wearing a question mark, and a judge hears it as a speech and marks you down for it. Ask one thing at a time. Start with questions you already know the answer to and walk forward from there, because the answers you already own are the floor you stand on. Get the closed question first, a yes or a number on the record, and only then ask the open one that makes them explain. And when an answer helps you, do not celebrate it and do not argue with it. Write it down, say thank you, ask the next one. The place to use it is your next speech, in front of the judge, where it counts.

In the answering chair. Answer the question that was asked, and answer it in your first sentence. Every extra sentence after that is free material you are handing to the person who is trying to beat you: they will take the loosest thing you said and build their next question out of it. Short is safe. If the question smuggles in something you do not accept, do not swallow it and do not ignore it; name it in one clause and then answer, like saying you would not call it that, and then giving your number. I do not know is a perfectly legal answer and it costs far less than a guess that gets caught two questions later. You may ask for a question to be repeated once. Never answer a question you did not actually understand.

The clock belongs to both of you. When the sand runs out the questioner stops asking, even mid-question, and the person answering finishes the sentence they are in and stops. Finishing on time is a skill, not a punishment, and both of you get exactly the same minute.

Today you are cross-examined on something real: the price you chose in this week's Build hour, with the table in front of you. Nobody is asking whether you like the price. They are asking where the number came from, and the honest answer lives in your own numbers, which is why the table sits on the desk beside you.

Then the question the week has been walking toward, and the motion you are about to argue: is it wrong to sell something for more than it cost to make? You have real skin in this one. In two weeks strangers are going to hand you money over a table, and the difference between what a unit cost you and what they pay is the entire reason there is a shop at all. Argue it properly, both ways, before you find out which side you are on.

steps.title: One minute in each chair
steps.body:
Set the table up like a real cross-examination: both of you standing, facing the room rather than each other, because in a real round you answer to the judge and not to your opponent. The one minute sand timer sits where both of you can see it. A third person turns it, or you turn it and trust each other, which is its own small lesson.

Round one, you in the answering chair. Your parent gets one minute to attack the price you chose, and they should not go easy. Questions that ought to be asked, and which you can prepare for right now by finding each answer in your own papers:

What does one unit cost you in materials? What did you spend before you had made a single one? How many do you have to sell before you have all of that money back? How many did you actually make in the production run? Is your break-even count smaller than the number written on your box, and what happens if it is not? Why not a dollar cheaper? Why not a dollar dearer? Where did the numbers in your demand table come from, and what would make you change your price on the day?

Answer each one in a sentence, off the table, with the number said out loud. If a question asks something your papers cannot answer, say so plainly and say what you would have to do to find out. That answer scores better than an invented one, every time.

Round two, you in the asking chair. Your parent now claims your price is wrong, and picks a direction: too dear, or too cheap. They get one sentence to say so. Then you get one minute of short questions, and your job is not to shout them down but to find the number their claim is standing on. Ask what they think you would sell at their price. Ask where that number came from. Ask what your profit would be if they were right, then ask them to work it out on your table, out loud.

Between the two rounds, one small thing worth noticing: which chair felt harder, and whether your answers got shorter in the second half of your minute or longer. They should get shorter.
checklist: The sand timer was visible to both of us and neither of us kept talking past it
I answered every question in my first sentence and read the real number off my table
I said I do not know at least once, or I can honestly say no question needed it
In the asking chair every question of mine was short enough to say in one breath
I asked what number their claim was standing on, rather than just disagreeing with it

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record the minute where you are being cross-examined, in one take, standing, with your profit table in shot. Then keep rolling for the week's question, answered in your own words with a reason attached: is it wrong to sell something for more than it cost to make, and does your answer change when the thing sold is somebody's whole day of work rather than a bag of materials?
